subject: Physiology
summary: The countercurrent multiplier in the nephron creates a steep medullary osmotic gradient that enables the kidney to concentrate urine and conserve water. It relies on the interaction of descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle.

sections.p: The kidney concentrates urine by generating an osmotic gradient in the medulla. The loop of Henle acts as a countercurrent multiplier, turning a small solute difference into a large gradient.
b: Essential for water balance and plasma osmolality
Explains why urine can be much more concentrated than plasma

sections.p: The descending limb is permeable to water but not solutes; the ascending limb actively pumps Na⁺, K⁺, and Cl⁻ out while being water‑impermeable. Flow in opposite directions creates a multiplier effect.
b: Active NaCl transport in thick ascending limb (NKCC2)
Passive water loss in descending limb creates hyperosmolar medulla

t.b: Does the kidney generate a concentrating gradient? High osmolality (>800 mOsm/kg) confirms an intact multiplier.
Is there a systemic water deficit? Low serum Na (<135 mmol/L) suggests dilutional states despite a functional multiplier.

sections.p: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water permeability of the collecting duct, allowing the gradient created by the multiplier to be used for water reabsorption.
b: ADH acts on V2 receptors → aquaporin‑2 insertion
Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) inhibit NKCC2, blunting the gradient

t.b: Is ADH appropriately secreted? Low ADH with high serum osmolality indicates central diabetes insipidus.

sections.p: Failure of the multiplier leads to an inability to concentrate urine, causing polyuria and risk of dehydration. Causes include tubular damage, chronic diuretic use, and genetic defects.
b: Acute tubular necrosis – loss of active Na⁺ transport
Loop diuretic overuse – pharmacologic inhibition of NKCC2

t.b: Is the tubule reabsorbing Na⁺? High FENa (>2%) suggests tubular dysfunction.

sections.p: Understanding the multiplier guides fluid management, diuretic choice, and interpretation of urine concentration tests in conditions like diabetes insipidus, heart failure, and severe dehydration.
b: In dehydration, a high urine osmolality confirms a functional multiplier and appropriate ADH response
In diabetes insipidus, low urine osmolality despite high serum osmolality signals a failed ADH pathway

t.b: Distinguishes central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; a rise in osmolality after desmopressin indicates central cause.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: the loop’s orientation, selective permeability, NKCC2 role, ADH effect on collecting duct, and how loop diuretics disrupt the gradient.
b: ADH acts downstream, not on the loop itself

whenToSeekHelp: Severe polyuria with dehydration and serum sodium >150 mmol/L (hypernatremic crisis)
Unexplained persistent low urine osmolality despite high serum osmolality (possible diabetes insipidus)
Acute kidney injury with rising creatinine and inability to concentrate urine

faq.q: Why can the kidney produce urine more concentrated than plasma?
faq.a: The countercurrent multiplier creates a medullary osmotic gradient that draws water out of the collecting duct when ADH is present.

faq.q: What drug directly blocks the countercurrent multiplier?
faq.a: Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, flattening the gradient.

faq.q: How does diabetes insipidus affect the multiplier?
faq.a: ADH deficiency or resistance prevents water reabsorption in the collecting duct, so the gradient is unused and urine remains dilute.

exam: Explain how the descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle differ in permeability and transport, and why this creates a gradient.
Describe the effect of ADH on urine concentration and how it interacts with the countercurrent multiplier.
A patient has polyuria, serum Na 152 mmol/L, and urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis and why?
